title: Clinton-appointed judge who blocked Trump legal moves dies at 92 - Whatfinger News Quick Hits
text:
Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who repeatedly rejected President Trump’s bids to shift his New York criminal case into federal court and was overseeing the Maduro prosecution, has died at 92.
A spokesperson for the Southern District of New York confirmed the death of U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, CBS News reported. He was 92 and had served nearly three decades on the federal bench in New York.
Fox News reported that Hellerstein died of natural causes on Tuesday. At the time of his death he was still listed as the judge presiding over the criminal case against former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro.
President Bill Clinton appointed Hellerstein in 1998, when the judge was 64. He spent the years that followed handling high-profile civil and criminal matters in one of the nation’s busiest federal courts, including major lawsuits tied to the Sept. 11 attacks and litigation connected to abuse at Iraq’s Abu Ghraib prison.
In recent years he became best known for a string of rulings against Trump. Those decisions kept a New York state criminal case in state court, limited presidential-immunity arguments, and checked an administration effort to use a wartime statute for deportations. That record fits a broader pattern in which Democratic-appointed judges have slowed or blocked enforcement priorities, including fights over IRS-ICE data sharing.
Trump’s removal bids stopped in federal court
Trump’s New York case centered on reimbursements to former attorney Michael Cohen for money paid to adult-film actress Stephanie Clifford, known as Stormy Daniels, just before the 2016 election. A state jury later found Trump guilty. His lawyers tried more than once to pull the matter into the Southern District of New York, arguing the conduct involved official acts.
Hellerstein refused. The New York Post noted that in an April 2023 ruling he wrote that hush money paid to an adult film star is not related to a president’s official acts.
In written opinions he went further, rejecting the claim that the reimbursements and related bookkeeping were constitutional duties of the presidency.
Hellerstein wrote:
“Reimbursing Cohen for advancing hush money to Stephanie Clifford cannot be considered the performance of a constitutional duty,”
He continued in the same opinion:
“Falsifying business records to hide such reimbursement, and to transform the reimbursement into a business expense for Trump and income to Cohen, likewise does not relate to a presidential duty.”
After the Supreme Court’s 2024 presidential-immunity ruling upended multiple Trump cases, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ordered Hellerstein to reexamine the immunity arguments. On Aug. 28 he again ruled against Trump, stating that the trial evidence does not infringe on presidential immunity.
He put it plainly in that order:
“the trial evidence does not infringe on presidential immunity.”
Breitbart reported that Hellerstein rejected three attempts by Trump to move the hush-money criminal case into federal court. Those losses left the prosecution in state court and left Trump without the federal forum his lawyers sought.
Alien Enemies Act ruling hit deportation plans
Hellerstein also ruled last year against the Trump administration’s use of the Alien Enemies Act in a case involving the deportation of Venezuelans. He held that the executive still had to meet due-process requirements built into the statute.
In that matter he stressed that the law itself imposes duties on the courts, not only on the executive. Breitbart quoted his language pointing to the statute’s demand for a full examination and hearing, and for removal only upon sufficient cause.
Lower-court limits on removal policy have become a recurring theme. The administration has had to take border and deportation fights higher, including efforts to win Supreme Court clearance to restart third-country deportations after trial judges narrowed the government’s options.
Maduro case now heads to a new judge
At his death Hellerstein was overseeing the criminal case against Nicolás Maduro. He had handled related matters connected to Maduro since 2014 and took on the current case in January, days after turning 92. That assignment drew some criticism because of his age.
Maduro’s attorney, Barry Pollack, sent a text message offering condolences.
“We were saddened to learn of Judge Hellerstein’s passing and offer our condolences to his family.”
Lawyer and former federal prosecutor Duncan Levin said the death is unlikely to create major delay. A new judge will need time to learn the file, but existing dates can stay or be adjusted.
Levin told reporters:
“There’s no automatic pause, and there’s really no fixed period of delay. Obviously a new judge is going to need time to get familiar with the case, but they can keep all the existing dates on the calendar or adjust them as necessary,”
He added that reading large volumes of paper is part of the job:
“One of the main qualifications of being a judge is that you can read a lot of paper. The fact that there’s extra paperwork falls into their skill set.”
Fox News reported that a new judge will be randomly assigned to Hellerstein’s other pending matters. That process will decide who inherits not only Maduro but the rest of a docket built over decades.
Age, workload, and a long Clinton-era tenure
Hellerstein’s final years on the bench were busy and closely watched. Months before the Maduro assignment, reporters covering the trial of Charlie Javice observed him appearing to briefly fall asleep. Javice, then 32, was convicted of defrauding JPMorgan in the $175 million sale of her startup.
He also presided over a federal lawsuit against Harvey Weinstein and the trial of David Hu. The through-line was a heavy caseload at an advanced age, capped by the decision to take Maduro’s case just after his 92nd birthday.
Clinton’s choice in 1998 produced nearly 30 years of SDNY service. In that time Hellerstein became one of the judges Trump’s lawyers had to clear, and repeatedly could not, when they tried to federalize the New York criminal case or expand immunity theories after the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision.
Similar clashes continue elsewhere. Biden-appointed judges have berated administration officials in open court and halted remaining DHS-funded ads, while other courts have blocked border infrastructure until higher courts step in, as in the fight over Big Bend border barriers.
Hellerstein’s Alien Enemies Act decision and his refusals to move the New York case sat in that same lane: trial-level power used to constrain a Republican administration’s legal strategy. For readers tracking the courts, his death removes one consistent vote against those moves and shifts the Maduro file to whatever judge the random wheel selects next.
Democratic presidents stocked the trial bench for a generation. Cases change hands when judges pass away, but the record those judges leave, on immigration statutes, criminal removals, and immunity, still shapes what the executive can do until voters and higher courts say otherwise.
